bib.title: RoboCat: A Self-Improving Generalist Agent for Robotic Manipulation

legacy_report:
SOURCE: RoboCat: A Self-Improving Generalist Agent for Robotic Manipulation, Bousmalis et al. (Google DeepMind), TMLR 12/2023.
COVERAGE: Pages 23-60 of 60 read (extracted chars 71399-170395 of 170395). Pages 23-29 are the reference list, skimmed for names only. Pages 1-22 were not re-read (previous pass). There is no separate safety or ethics section in 23-60. The only such content is the model card (p30). Figure pages (12-28) have captions and axis labels only, with no bar values in the extraction. The text of Tables 5-21 extracted cleanly.

CLAIMS (ranked; all appendix material, pp30-60)
- Self-generated data pipeline: humans give a few demos, a RoboCat agent is fine-tuned on 500 or 1000 successful episodes, it collects more data autonomously, and the final generalist trains on both.
  number: 500 or 1000 episodes; "over 4000 hours" of human demos, over 100 participants
  setup: real-robot tasks, Sawyer 5-DoF and Panda 7-DoF
  quote: "we fine-tuned a RoboCat agent on 500 or 1000 successful episodes, as explained in Section 2.1.2. We then used this specialised agent to gather, autonomously, more data for the same task variation. This self-generated RoboCat data, combined with all demonstrations that ended up being collected for that task variation, were used to train our final RoboCat agent."
  where: p36, B.2
- Self-generated data is mostly failures, and much of it exceeds the human data in volume. The self-improvement tasks use previous RoboCat versions, not the final one.
  number: Table 8 (human successes / failures; agent successes / failures)
    - Panda apple: 1956/121; 8117/6058
    - Panda banana: 2320/90; 4556/6352
    - Panda peach: 2200/98; 2409/11125
    - Panda strawberry: 2052/137; 195/2171
    - Sawyer stacking BG: 424/0; 4159/3853
    - Sawyer tower RBG: 926/1821; 4718/7776
    - Sawyer inverted pyramid: 1409/1510; 1081/11155
    - Sawyer vegetables, e.g. pepper: 1938/2317; 2217/7122
  setup: real robots, self-improvement tasks
  quote: "Table 8: Quantities of human demonstrations and self-generated data." The agent-trajectory columns hold the numbers above.
  where: p38
- The final model roughly matches the success rate of its training data on self-improvement tasks and beats it in some cases (banana, peach, strawberry, potato). Failed self-generated episodes count in the training-data rate, but failed demos do not.
  number: no per-task values in the text. The values are in the Figure 24/25 bars only, which the extraction does not give.
  quote: "On average RoboCat performance matches the success rate of the training data, overcoming it in some cases (see lifting banana, peach, strawberry Figure 24 and potato Figure 25)."
  where: p53 (G.1.1)
- Where RoboCat sees the same information as the data-generating expert (real tasks), it can beat the expert. In sim the experts used privileged state, so RoboCat falls short, by 10% or less except on tower building.
  quote: "the vision-based RoboCat generalist has a performance reduction of 10% or less compared to the state-based single-task experts (Figure 20), for all families except tower building." and "when RoboCat has access to same information as the experts that generated the data, as for the real tasks Figure 21, it is able to overcome the performance of the agents generating data."
  where: p51
- More fine-tuning demos help, but not uniformly, and insertion stays hard (Table 15, success at 500 / 1000 demos):
    - KUKA gear lift: 56% / 86%
    - Shape insertion: circle 7% / 19%, pentagon 6% / 10%, square 4% / 11%
    - Shape removal: circle 47% / 72%, pentagon 87% / 94%, square 75% / 79%
    - Bowl insertion: lemon 84% / 82%, peach 76% / 86%, strawberry 92% / 84%
    - Bowl removal: lemon 60% / 62%, peach 69% / 76%, strawberry 64% / 77%
  Two of the three bowl insertion cases go down from 500 to 1000 demos.
  setup: Panda/KUKA real, fine-tuned from the generalist
  quote: "fine-tuning on more demonstrations in general improves performance, sometimes reaching similar performance as the human teleoperators. This does not apply to the insert tasks, which result very challenging for our agents due to the required reorientation and shape understanding."
  where: p52-53
- Fine-tuning recipe and data weighting. Fine-tuning uses only successful episodes, and failures are used only in generalist training.
  quote: "When fine-tuning to a limited number of demonstrations, we find best performance when only training on successful episodes." Also: "For fine-tuning we use the Adam optimiser ... constant learning rate of 1e−5 ... We train for up to 50 000 gradient steps." Generalist: "every task variant is sampled equally ... failed episodes and successful episodes are also sampled equally."
  where: p47
- Model size: the 1.18B model beats the 364M model most on hard tasks.
  number: 6-21% improvement
  setup: sim structure-building, RoboCat-lim
  quote: "the larger model yields an improvement of 6-21% in the success rate for the different task families. In particular, while the smaller model only slightly degrades performance for the easier stacking tasks, it is much poorer for the more challenging pyramid and tower-building tasks."
  where: p53
- Baseline VFMs (59 fine-tuned combos, behaviour cloning) collapse at low data (Table 17, final_success):
    - 500 demos, panda stacking BG: 0.01-0.36
    - 1000 demos, inverted pyramid and tower GRB: 0.00 for all models
    - more than 10 000 demos: 0.51-0.93 on stacking
  setup: top eight models reported
  quote: "We fine-tuned a total of 59 combinations ... Since the non-frozen pretrained model performed much better, we only report the results for non-frozen models."
  where: p55-58
- VQ-GAN tokeniser vs patch ResNet (1.18B): the patch ResNet is better on training tasks but worse on held-out tasks. Small-scale ablation (62M, sim Panda RGB stacking, with hindsight goals only, evaluated from the goal trajectory's first state):
    - Predicting pixels instead of tokens gives zero success on held-out tasks.
    - Predicting k=5 steps ahead is best, with +50% relative generalisation over k=0.
    - Larger VQ-GAN vocabulary hurts generalisation.
  quote: "we see a 50% relative improvement in generalisation performance as we increase k from 0 to 5. Further increase in prediction horizon results in performance degradation." and "the policy learnt by predicting pixels fails (zero success rate) as it seems to ignore the goal" and "the generalisation ability monotonically declines as we increase V."
  where: p45-46
- Positive transfer, NIST-i insertion (364M model, real, Table 18): fixed base 64%, inverted fixed base 40%, moving base 38%. Insert/remove: fixed 64%/100%, moving 38%/97%.
  quote: "moving from the 364M model to the full RoboCat agent eliminates just under two thirds of the gear insertion failures in both the fixed base and the moving base setting" (error 0.36 to 0.13; 0.62 to 0.23). A specialist BC control gives 8% fixed vs 13% moving, i.e. "No evidence for data bias."
  where: p59-60
- Extra cameras: for specialist BC, 2 to 4 cameras (adding wrist cameras) raises insert from 13% to 36% and remove from 24% to 54%. RoboCat itself uses two basket cameras.
  where: p60
- Human teleoperator success rates give a ceiling for the real data (Table 10): Panda stacking 96.5%, gear insert 76.7%, Sawyer tower 50.0%, inverted pyramid 52.6%, vegetable lifting 63.2%.
  quote: "We noticed that on-site teleoperators achieve higher success rates than their remote counterparts"; "these 'shuffle' episodes made our agents more robust."
  where: p35, p38
- Per-task training results (Table 15), real tasks that did not reach high success: Sawyer tower RGB triplet 5 23%, inverted pyramid 17%, apple lifting 40%. Sim Panda tower triplet 5 RBG 34%.
  where: p52

LIMITS
- Single model per setting. Quote: "The reported values do not take into consideration model uncertainty as they are evaluations of a single model and its ablations. It is prohibitive for us to evaluate models from multiple training runs".
- Evaluation uses 100 episodes (25 for checkpoint selection). The best checkpoint is picked on 25-episode runs, then re-evaluated.
- Real-task success is counted visually, not by learned detectors (about 90% accuracy). Real RGB evaluation used a different success criterion from Lee et al. (2021), with the baselines recounted visually.
- Appendix G describes the self-improvement loop for a single round. Table 8 and the text show no per-round numbers and no ablation of self-generated data vs demos alone in this part. Fig 24/25 compare only against the success rate of the training data.
- Insertion tasks are poor (shape insertion 4-19%).
- Weights for NIST-i (3x) and sim (halved after 1M steps) were "preventive": "keeping all weights equal may have also been effective."
- Model card: "not been evaluated for deployment and safety"; "interaction of diverse training data domains and the different affordances ... is poorly understood".

BUILDS ON: MPO (Abdolmaleki et al. 2018) for RL experts. Lee et al. (2021), RGB Stacking benchmark, sim-to-real and offline RL. Reed et al. (2022), Gato (patch ResNet tokeniser baseline). Esser et al. (2021) VQ-GAN and van den Oord et al. (2017) VQ. Abramson et al. (2021), teleop web UI. He et al. (2022), MAE decoder idea. Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) AdamW. Kimble et al. (2020), NIST benchmark.

CODE: none.
